story_text.value:
I wanted a p2p file transfer site that didn't require you to create an account or login, didn't require you to upload your files and either established a webrtc p2p connection or just failed (no TURN relay). You're data never hits the peeryeet server.

For the hackernews audience I'll mention my other requirements: a single binary, written in C, super efficient so I can run the whole service on a very minimal VM.

Hopefully I can finally stop sharing files with myself via gmail now. :)

story_text.value:
This project doesn't solve a burning problem for me, but it's more of a curiosity-driven experiment asking one question: with LLMs and fuzzing, how close can I get to a 100% Excel-compatible spreadsheet engine?

After working on this for a couple of months, it seems to be pretty close now (and in some cases, more accurate than Excel). Recent fuzzing runs have been unable to find discrepancies with Excel, but I think that there is still a long tail of cases out there. Nonetheless, visi has worked well so far for casual agentic use cases, e.g. modeling the minimum spend to break even on a credit card annual fee/running a DCF model for a company. To view the resulting workbook, I've been using this OOXML viewer (HN link): https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=48436863

Note: the name "visi" is a nod to VisiCalc. It is also easy to type.

story_text.value:
Hi All - I've been missing Winamp for a long time and could not find a simple, fast audio player for macOS that I liked.

So, I built Vibe. It's a fast, minimal music file player for Mac. It's written in Objective-C and optimized heavily for speed, resource use, and quality. ~12Mb app. No accounts, telemetry, or bloat.

It's free and open source: https://github.com/cmicali/vibe

Also available on the Mac App Store if you prefer: https://apps.apple.com/us/app/vibe-music-player/id1582482361...

I started this before "Vibe" had it's meaning changed, so it was completely hand-written for the first 4-5 years. Now I am using agents to speed up progress and implement things I otherwise wouldn't have had the time to do.

I would love any feedback, ideas, feature requests etc.

story_text.value:
I started Solarite several years ago because I wanted something simpler to use than the existing js ui frameworks. Features like:

- not having to setup a build environment or wait for compilation

- no signals or other dance to setup my data

- class based components, where I could pass arguments to sub-components as constructor args

- scoped styles, two-way binding and other nice to haves.

- not having the limitations of shadow dom (Lit)

- Just be a library I can import anywhere, not be a whole framework.

I wasn't able to find anything that did all of the above. It has a score of 1.08 on the js-framework-benchmark, which is faster than just about every widely known competitor, and most of the faster ones have implementation note "penalties" for not conforming to the benchmark requirements.

Source: https://github.com/eric-frost/solarite Docs: https://eric-frost.github.io/solarite/docs/ Js-Framework-Benchmark: https://krausest.github.io/js-framework-benchmark/current.ht...

I've used Solarite in production for a few years for an internal work project, but I could use more feedback on the API before I feel comfortable releasing version 1.0.

story_text.value:
Kio is a statically typed, hosted language that is designed to be ultra-portable. Kio 0.1 supports eight host languages and more will be added in the coming weeks.

Kio is based on polymorphic lambda calculus with higher-kinded types. Kio has type-driven macros (elaborators) and it can statically check asserted equivalences using a normalizer.

Kio is a minimalistic language. It doesn't have built-in effectful functions and it doesn't even have built-in string or numeric types. Instead programs declare the capabilities they need and the host supplies them.

The language is designed with AI, which is bound to raise some eyebrows, so I blogged about that here: https://jdevuyst.github.io/kio/blog/2026-10-01-introducing-k...

title.value: Show HN: The Kio Programming Language

story_text.value:
Hi all! I made a 311 byte Klotski solver in C++

So back when I first got to use a mobile phone in 2012 I used to play a lot of puzzle games. These were notoriously hard to solve (on high levels), and I always wondered how are these created, how do they find the minimum moves, how do they know its even minimal.

Now after being in a CS major for over 3 years, I finally understand these systems fairly. So I decided to make a klotski solver.

I wanted to make it fun so I stored the whole game board in an integer (uint64_t), as I like integers more than vectors. And then I got the urge to minify the engine to the max extent I could, so shrunk it down to 311 bytes from ~3.5 KB. The engine is only the searching part though.

The solver is a BFS that explores every reachable position. For the classic start it finds the best solution in 116 moves, after exploring all 25,955 reachable states in about 2-4 ms.

Here's the repo; any feedback is welcomed : ) https://github.com/Dream-World-Coder/depuzzled

story_text.value:
Was tired of every good markdown editor out there being electron and their consuming 500mb + 3% CPU when idle(!) when they're just editing text.

So I built one from scratch in pure native. * Launches in 0.1s * Takes 0.0% CPU when idle * Consumes 50MB memory even with a large workspace open * Binary is 15MB * Supports all markdown — LaTeX, Mermaid, tables, image attachments etc * Fully open source, GPLv3 license

Hat tip to writer.computer which inspired the idea!
